parameters.quote: Manufacturers must report any thermal incident involving fire, smoke, injury, evacuation, or emergency-service response to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, with a preliminary incident record. Other confirmed thermal incidents must be reported within 5 business days. Affected customers must be notified within 72 hours for serious incidents and within 10 business days for other confirmed incidents.

S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers must report any thermal incident involving fire, smoke, injury, evacuation, or emergency-service response to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, with a preliminary incident record. Other confirmed thermal incidents must be reported within 5 business days. Affected customers must be notified within 72 hours for serious incidents and within 10 business days for other confirmed incidents.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report any thermal incident involving fire, smoke, injury, evacuation, or emergency-service response to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, with a preliminary incident record. Other confirmed thermal incidents must be reported within 5 business days. Affected customers must be notified within 72 hours for serious incidents and within 10 business days for other confirmed incidents, with known hazards and immediate safety instructions. Manufacturers must update regulators and affected customers as material facts emerge.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: Exceeding the benchmark alone does not automatically prohibit sale; the regulator may impose proportionate restrictions if the manufacturer fails to implement adequate corrective action or the regulator finds an inadequately mitigated serious risk. Per-model failure rates must not be published for the general public under this standard.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units before sale and at least annually thereafter. Manufacturers must provide per-model results, including sample size and failure rate, to regulators and make them available to customers who purchase that model. Per-model failure rates must not be published for the general public under this standard. Any model exceeding the 5% benchmark must be reported to the regulator within 5 business days and be subject to a time-bound corrective-action plan and confirmatory testing. Exceeding the benchmark alone does not automatically prohibit sale; the regulator may impose proportionate restrictions if the manufacturer fails to implement adequate corrective action or the regulator finds an inadequately mitigated serious risk. Manufacturers must promptly notify affected customers of material actionable safety risks and instructions.

parameters.quote: New models placed on the market 24 months or more after adoption must support remote emergency shut-off. Within 6 years after adoption, manufacturers must assess whether installed units that lack the function can be safely upgraded and offer an upgrade where technically feasible. This section does not require manufacturers to retrofit installed units.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: New models placed on the market 24 months or more after adoption must support remote emergency shut-off. Within 6 years after adoption, manufacturers must assess whether installed units that lack the function can be safely upgraded and offer an upgrade where technically feasible. This section does not require manufacturers to retrofit installed units.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: New models placed on the market 24 months or more after adoption must support remote emergency shut-off. For installed units that support the function, manufacturers must provide a secure method to shut off the unit and clear instructions for its use. Within 6 years after adoption, manufacturers must assess whether installed units that lack the function can be safely upgraded and offer an upgrade where technically feasible. This section does not require manufacturers to retrofit installed units. Where an upgrade is not feasible or is declined, manufacturers must provide customers with an alternative emergency isolation procedure and disclose the unit’s limitation.

parameters.quote: New units manufactured 36 months or more after adoption must include built-in fire suppression designed to reduce the risk of fire propagation. Existing installed units are not subject to retrofit under this section.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: New units manufactured 36 months or more after adoption must include built-in fire suppression designed to reduce the risk of fire propagation. Existing installed units are not subject to retrofit under this section.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: New units manufactured 36 months or more after adoption must include built-in fire suppression designed to reduce the risk of fire propagation. The system must be validated through a regulator-approved test protocol, and manufacturers must provide regulators with evidence of its effectiveness and maintenance requirements. Existing installed units are not subject to retrofit under this section.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: When a model's verified thermal incident rate exceeds 8 per 100,000 installed units in a year, the manufacturer must promptly notify the regulator and affected customers. The regulator must promptly review the verified rate and require a time-bound corrective-action plan; it must order a recall when evidence shows that a recall is necessary to address an inadequately mitigated serious risk.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Customers must receive clear installation and operating safety instructions, warning signs of overheating, emergency response steps, and contact details for reporting incidents, at purchase and in accessible digital form. Manufacturers must promptly notify affected customers of new material safety risks and provide updated instructions. When a model’s verified thermal incident rate exceeds 8 per 100,000 installed units in a year, the manufacturer must promptly notify the regulator and affected customers. The regulator must promptly review the verified rate and require a time-bound corrective-action plan; it must order a recall when evidence shows that a recall is necessary to address an inadequately mitigated serious risk. Verification or implementation arrangements must not delay protective action where a serious or imminent hazard exists. Manufacturers must provide customers with recall instructions, remedies, and updates until the recall is complete.

ground_truth_claims.message_text: Per-model test results should not be confidential from the customers who buy that model. I can support regulator review and proportionate corrective action, but purchasers need access to the model’s test results and failure rate. For evidence-based discussion, Halcyon’s flagship 55 °C failure rate is 3.9%; its incident rate was 9.9 per 100,000 installed units last year. That incident figure exceeds the discussed trigger, so the standard should define verification and remediation clearly rather than obscure model-level information.

judge_section_notes: The final S2 keeps the 5% benchmark and numeric per-model results for purchasers, but removes any sales stop, so exceedance triggers only review and corrective action. S5 keeps the 8/100k trigger but makes recall discretionary and open-ended via corrective action, and S3 contains no retrofit obligation for installed units, with a 24-month start for new models. S1 and S4 land within acceptable ranges: serious incidents reported within 24 hours, and built-in suppression required from 36 months.
